proofs.proof_tex:
Fix \(\theta=(\theta_{dj})\in\mathcal T_K(r)\).  By \(\mathrm{def{:}finite\mbox{-}array\mbox{-}experiment}\), the observable law \(P_\theta\) is the law of
\[
 \mathcal O_K=((Z_{di},Y_{di}):d\in\{0,1\},\ 1\le i\le n_d),
\]
where the two arms are independent, the observations are independent within arms, and, for every \(d,i,j\),
\[
 P_\theta(Z_{di}=j)=K^{-1},\qquad
 P_\theta(Y_{di}=1\mid Z_{di}=j)=p_{dj}.
 \tag{1}
\]
Thus \(P_\theta\) identifies every \(p_{dj}\), since every cell in (1) has positive probability.  The causal quantity is not defined to equal an observed functional.  Rather, for a compatible collection \(\pi=(\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_K)\), where \(\pi_j\) is a coupling on \(\{0,1\}^2\) with marginals \(\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p_{0j})\) and \(\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p_{1j})\), define
\[
 \tau(\pi)=\frac1K\sum_{j=1}^K
 \int_{\{0,1\}^2}|y_1-y_0|\,d\pi_j(y_0,y_1).
 \tag{2}
\]
The identified set under the maintained cellwise-marginal restrictions is
\[
 \Theta_I(P_\theta)=\{\tau(\pi):\pi_j\in
 \Pi(\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p_{0j}),
      \operatorname{Bernoulli}(p_{1j})),\ 1\le j\le K\}.
 \tag{3}
\]

We compute (3) by the binary extremal-coupling technique.  Put
\(Q_j=\pi_j\{(1,1)\}\).  The four atoms of \(\pi_j\) are
\[
 Q_j,\qquad p_{0j}-Q_j,\qquad p_{1j}-Q_j,
 \qquad 1-p_{0j}-p_{1j}+Q_j.
\]
Their nonnegativity is equivalent to
\[
 \max\{0,p_{0j}+p_{1j}-1\}
 \le Q_j\le \min\{p_{0j},p_{1j}\}.                 \tag{4}
\]
Conversely, every \(Q_j\) in (4) makes the four displayed atoms nonnegative and summing to one, so (4) is also sufficient for a coupling with the prescribed marginals.  Its mismatch probability is
\[
 t_j:=\int |y_1-y_0|\,d\pi_j
 =p_{0j}+p_{1j}-2Q_j.                              \tag{5}
\]
As \(Q_j\) traverses (4), (5) traverses the full interval
\[
 |p_{1j}-p_{0j}|\le t_j\le
 \min\{p_{0j}+p_{1j},\,2-p_{0j}-p_{1j}\}.         \tag{6}
\]
The Cartesian product of the cellwise intervals in (6), followed by the linear average in (2), has image equal to the interval
\[
 \Theta_I(P_\theta)=
 \left[
  \frac1K\sum_{j=1}^K|p_{1j}-p_{0j}|,
  \frac1K\sum_{j=1}^K
  \min\{p_{0j}+p_{1j},2-p_{0j}-p_{1j}\}
 \right].                                         \tag{7}
\]
Indeed, the image is convex because the domain is a product of intervals, and its two endpoints are attained by taking every \(Q_j\) at the corresponding endpoint of (4).  Hence (7) is sharp, not merely an outer bound.  Its lower endpoint is the observable-law functional
\[
 L_K=\frac1K\sum_{j=1}^K|p_{1j}-p_{0j}|.          \tag{8}
\]

It remains to derive the advertised affine formula.  The support restrictions give \(0<b<a<1/2\) and \(\theta_{dj}\in\{-1,1\}\).  Therefore
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 |p_{1j}-p_{0j}|
 &=|b\theta_{1j}-a\theta_{0j}|\\
 &=\begin{cases}
    a-b,&\theta_{0j}\theta_{1j}=1,\\
    a+b,&\theta_{0j}\theta_{1j}=-1,
   \end{cases}\\
 &=a-b\theta_{0j}\theta_{1j}.                    \tag{9}
 \end{aligned}
\]
Averaging (9), using the declared definition
\(\rho_K=K^{-1}\sum_j\theta_{0j}\theta_{1j}\), and comparing with (8) yields
\[
 L_K=a-b\rho_K.                                   \tag{10}
\]
Thus the equality of the causal sharp endpoint and the observed-law functional follows from the coupling constraints (4)--(7), rather than being imposed by definition.

Throughout the proof, total variation is the supremum over measurable events.  Two elementary consequences will be used with their constants exposed.  If \(0\le g\le B\), then the layer-cake representation gives
\[
 |\mathbb E_Pg-\mathbb E_Qg|
 \le\int_0^B|P(g>t)-Q(g>t)|\,dt
 \le B\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}.             \tag{11}
\]
If \(\mathsf K\) is a Markov kernel, integrating each transition probability, which takes values in \([0,1]\), and applying the same layer-cake argument gives
\[
 \lVert P\mathsf K-Q\mathsf K\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}
 \le\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}.              \tag{12}
\]
These are the bounded-expectation and data-processing steps used below.

Define
\[
 e_K=\min\{1,5\varepsilon_K+\eta_K\},\qquad
 \delta_K=2s_K+2/K,
\]
\[
 u_K=e_K+\min\{1,\lambda_Kc\delta_K/2\},
 \qquad
 d_K=\min\{1,5\varepsilon_K+\lambda_K^2/(2K)\}.  \tag{13}
\]
We first compare the two honest-length frontiers at the finite intensity \(\lambda_K\).

Fix \(\zeta>0\), and choose \(\mathcal C_K\in\mathscr C_K\) with coverage at least \(1-\alpha\) for every \(\theta\in\mathcal T_K(r)\) and worst expected length at most \(C_{K,\alpha}+\zeta\).  For all sufficiently large \(K\), Proposition \(\mathrm{prop{:}supported\mbox{-}mixture\mbox{-}legality}\) makes \(q_K\) available.  Given \(\rho\in[-r,r]\), put \(q=q_K(\rho)\).  On the support of \(\Pi_{K,q}^{\mathrm{shell}}\), that proposition and Proposition \(\mathrm{prop{:}sharp\mbox{-}cot\mbox{-}endpoint}\) give
\[
 |q-\rho|\le\delta_K,
 \qquad |L_K-(a-bq)|\le bs_K.                     \tag{14}
\]
Integrating the finite-array coverage inequality over this supported law and expanding both endpoints of the reported interval by \(bs_K\), with clipping to \(\mathcal A\), therefore gives coverage of \(a-bq\) at least \(1-\alpha\) under \(P^{\mathrm{mix}}_{K,q}\).

For \(\rho,\rho'\in[-r,r]\), couple \(P^{\mathcal E}_{\lambda_K,\rho}\) and \(P^{\mathcal E}_{\lambda_K,\rho'}\) using the same Poisson count and the same independent uniforms for their marks.  One mark disagrees with probability \(c|\rho-\rho'|/2\).  Conditional union bound and then expectation over the Poisson count yield
\[
 \left\lVert P^{\mathcal E}_{\lambda_K,\rho}
 -P^{\mathcal E}_{\lambda_K,\rho'}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}
 \le \min\{1,\lambda_Kc|\rho-\rho'|/2\}.         \tag{15}
\]
Apply \(\mathcal C_K\) after the reverse kernel in Theorem \(\mathrm{thm{:}collision\mbox{-}comparison}\).  Equations (12), (14), and (15), followed by one further endpoint expansion of size \(b\delta_K\), show that under \(P^{\mathcal E}_{\lambda_K,\rho}\) the resulting interval covers \(a-b\rho\) with probability at least \(1-\alpha-u_K\).  Since every interval lies in \(\mathcal A\) and hence has length at most \(2br\), (11) and the two expansions bound its worst expected length by
\[
 C_{K,\alpha}+\zeta+2b(s_K+\delta_K)+2br,u_K.    \tag{16}
\]

We will use the following explicit coverage repair.  If an interval rule has coverage at least \(1-\alpha-u\), independently replace its output by \(\mathcal A\) with probability
\[
 \gamma(u)=\frac{u}{\alpha+u}.                    \tag{17}
\]
The assumptions \(\alpha>0\) and \(u\ge0\) make this division valid, and \(0\le\gamma(u)\le1\).  Its repaired coverage is at least
\[
 \gamma(u)+(1-\gamma(u))(1-\alpha-u)=1-\alpha,   \tag{18}
\]
while its expected length increases by at most \(2br\gamma(u)\).  Applying (17)--(18) with \(u=u_K\) to (16), then letting \(\zeta\downarrow0\), proves
\[
 C_\alpha(\lambda_K)
 \le C_{K,\alpha}+2b(s_K+\delta_K)+2br,u_K
       +\frac{2br,u_K}{\alpha+u_K}.              \tag{19}
\]

Conversely, take a marked-Poisson honest interval rule at intensity \(\lambda_K\) whose worst expected length is at most \(C_\alpha(\lambda_K)+\zeta\), and apply it to the deterministic collision statistic.  The deterministic part of Theorem \(\mathrm{thm{:}collision\mbox{-}comparison}\) bounds total variation by \(d_K\), uniformly over \(\theta\in\mathcal T_K(r)\).  Proposition \(\mathrm{prop{:}sharp\mbox{-}cot\mbox{-}endpoint}\) supplies the exact target equality \(L_K=a-b\rho_K\).  By (11), coverage falls by at most \(d_K\), and expected length rises by at most \(2brd_K\).  Applying (17)--(18) with \(u=d_K\), independently of the array, and letting \(\zeta\downarrow0\) gives
\[
 C_{K,\alpha}
 \le C_\alpha(\lambda_K)+2brd_K
       +\frac{2brd_K}{\alpha+d_K}.                \tag{20}
\]

The function \(\lambda\mapsto C_\alpha(\lambda)\) is continuous on \([0,\infty)\).  Indeed, couple counts at \(\lambda\) and \(\lambda'\) by starting with a Poisson count of intensity \(\min\{\lambda,\lambda'\}\) and adding an independent count of intensity \(|\lambda-\lambda'|\); use the same marking mechanism on the common points.  Uniformly in \(\rho\), the observations agree with probability at least \(e^{-|\lambda-\lambda'|}\).  Hence, writing
\[
 v(\lambda,\lambda')=1-e^{-|\lambda-\lambda'|},  \tag{21}
\]
transporting an honest rule in either direction loses at most \(v\) in coverage and changes expected length by at most \(2brv\).  The repair (17) in both directions proves
\[
 |C_\alpha(\lambda)-C_\alpha(\lambda')|
 \le 2brv(\lambda,\lambda')
 +\frac{2brv(\lambda,\lambda')}{\alpha+v(\lambda,\lambda')}, \tag{22}
\]
which tends to zero as \(\lambda'\to\lambda\).

Now suppose \(\lambda_K\to\lambda<\infty\).  Lemma \(\mathrm{lem{:}vanishing\mbox{-}triples\mbox{-}implies\mbox{-}growing\mbox{-}cells}\) gives \(K\to\infty\).  Boundedness of \(\lambda_K\) and the definition of \(s_K\) imply, eventually,
\[
 s_K=\{K(1\vee\lambda_K)\}^{-1/4}\to0,
 \qquad
 Ks_K^2=\sqrt{K/(1\vee\lambda_K)}\to\infty.       \tag{23}
\]
Consequently \(\eta_K=2e^{-Ks_K^2/2}\to0\), while Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}vanishing\mbox{-}triples}\) gives \(\varepsilon_K\to0\).  It follows from (13) and boundedness of \(\lambda_K\) that
\[
 e_K,\delta_K,u_K,d_K\longrightarrow0.             \tag{24}
\]
Combining (19), (20), (22), and (24) yields
\[
 C_{K,\alpha}\longrightarrow C_\alpha(\lambda).  \tag{25}
\]

We next certify the finite programs in \(\mathrm{def{:}certified\mbox{-}interval\mbox{-}lp}\).  The input domain is exactly the one declared there: \(\lambda\), nonrational grid points, and all other fixed reals are supplied by computable-real oracles.  Equation (15), with \(\lambda_K\) replaced by \(\lambda\), proves the stated likelihood modulus
\[
 \lVert f_{\lambda,\rho}-f_{\lambda,\rho'}\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}
 \le\omega_\lambda(|\rho-\rho'|)
 :=\min\{1,\lambda c|\rho-\rho'|/2\}.             \tag{26}
\]
By (11), the modulus for an event is \(\omega_\lambda\), and that for a \([0,2br]\)-valued length is \(2br\omega_\lambda\).

The stated tail certificate follows directly.  When \(\lambda=0\), \(\tau_m(0)=0\).  When \(0<\lambda<m+1\), exponential Markov inequality gives, for \(t>0\),
\[
 \Pr_\lambda(N\ge m+1)
 \le \exp\{\lambda(e^t-1)-t(m+1)\}.              \tag{27}
\]
The exponent is minimized at the positive value
\(t=\log((m+1)/\lambda)\), because its derivative is
\(\lambda e^t-(m+1)\).  Substitution yields
\[
 \tau_m(\lambda)
 \le e^{-\lambda}\left(\frac{e\lambda}{m+1}\right)^{m+1}. \tag{28}
\]

For the lower certificate, start with an arbitrary continuum-honest randomized interval rule.  On a retained state \(x\in\mathsf X_m\), and for each realization of its random interval, replace the interval by the shortest member of \(\mathsf A_h\) spanning exactly the grid targets it contains; if it contains none, use \(\varnothing_G\).  Grid-target membership is unchanged and length does not increase.  Deleting the overflow states removes probability \(\tau_m(\lambda)\), uniformly in \(\rho\), because the total count is \(\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda)\).  The induced weights therefore satisfy the exact lower program with objective no larger than the continuum rule's worst expected length.  In its directed rational relaxation, replacing coverage coefficients upward and the coverage right side downward enlarges the feasible set, while replacing length contributions downward cannot raise its objective.  Therefore
\[
 D_{m,h,s}^-\le C_\alpha(\lambda).                \tag{29}
\]

For the upper certificate, take an exact rational feasible solution of the directed upper program.  Downward rounding of retained coverage and overflow mass, together with upward rounding of \(1-\alpha\), implies that its actual coverage at every grid node is at least \(1-\alpha\).  Upward rounding of every length contribution implies that its actual expected length at every grid node is at most \(P_{m,h,s}^+\).  Give the overflow state the action \(\mathcal A\).  For arbitrary \(\rho\), choose a nearest grid point \(\rho_j\); the maximum-gap condition gives \(|\rho-\rho_j|\le h/2\).  If an unexpanded action covers \(a-b\rho_j\), its expansion \(E_h\) covers \(a-b\rho\).  By (26), the expanded rule has coverage at least \(1-\alpha-\omega_h\), where
\[
 \omega_h=\min\{1,\lambda ch/4\}.                \tag{30}
\]
The repair (17) with \(u=\omega_h\), namely with
\(\gamma_h=\omega_h/(\alpha+\omega_h)\), makes coverage at least \(1-\alpha\) for every \(\rho\in[-r,r]\).  Expansion adds at most \(bh\), transfer from \(\rho_j\) to \(\rho\) adds at most \(2br\omega_h\) to expected length by (11), and repair adds at most \(2br\gamma_h\).  Directed upper enclosure of each term therefore proves
\[
 C_\alpha(\lambda)
 \le P_{m,h,s}^++bh+2br\omega_h+2br\gamma_h
 =U_{m,h,s}^+.                                    \tag{31}
\]
Equations (29)--(31) are the advertised rational enclosure, and (30)--(31) certify continuum coverage rather than coverage only on the grid.

We now justify the word ``exact.''  After directed enclosure, each program has finitely many variables and rational coefficients.  The row-sum and nonnegativity constraints put the action weights in a finite product of simplices.  Since \(t\ge0\), and the full interval gives a finite feasible objective whenever the upper rounding is sufficiently fine, minimization may be restricted to a compact rational polytope.  A linear objective attains its minimum on a face containing a vertex.  Every vertex is obtained by solving one of finitely many square rational systems selected from the active constraints, so it is rational and finite basis enumeration finds the least objective exactly.  For the lower program, the same finite enumeration applied to the algebraic dual finds rational multipliers; primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and equality of the two rational objectives certify optimality by the identity
\[
 c^Tx-y^Tb
 =\text{a sum of products of nonnegative primal slacks and nonnegative dual multipliers}. \tag{32}
\]
Thus no floating-point output is a certificate.  For fixed \(m,h\), the aggregate directed error tends to zero with \(s\).  Once the total downward coverage error and upward right-side error are smaller than \(\alpha\), the rule that always reports \(\mathcal A\) is feasible for the directed upper program.  Hence the exact rational certificates exist for every fixed \(m,h\) and all sufficiently large \(s\).

It remains to prove contraction.  Let \(\xi_s\) be the largest, over the finitely many constraint rows, of the sum of all directed likelihood, tail, right-side, length, and correction-term enclosure widths affecting that row.  The aggregate budget in the definition gives a finite constant \(C_0\), depending only on the bounded fixed inputs, such that
\[
 0\le\xi_s\le C_0 2^{-s}\longrightarrow0.        \tag{33}
\]

Fix \(\zeta>0\), and take a continuum-honest rule with worst expected length at most \(C_\alpha(\lambda)+\zeta\).  Replace its action on overflow by \(\mathcal A\), which raises worst expected length by at most \(2br\tau_m\).  On retained states, round each interval endpoint outward to adjacent target-grid endpoints.  This preserves coverage, gives an action in \(\mathsf A_h\), and raises length by at most \(2bh\).  For large \(s\), mix this rule with \(\mathcal A\) with probability
\[
 \beta_s=2\xi_s/\alpha\le1.                       \tag{34}
\]
Before directed rounding, (34) creates gridwise coverage slack \(\alpha\beta_s=2\xi_s\), enough to absorb all aggregate coefficient and right-side errors.  The resulting weights are feasible for the rational upper program and have directed objective at most
\[
 C_\alpha(\lambda)+\zeta+2br\tau_m+2bh
 +2br\beta_s+\xi_s.                               \tag{35}
\]
Adding the expansion, modulus, repair, and directed correction terms from (31), then taking \(m\to\infty\), \(h\downarrow0\), and \(s\to\infty\), gives
\[
 \limsup U_{m,h,s}^+\le C_\alpha(\lambda)         \tag{36}
\]
after \(\zeta\downarrow0\).  Here (28) and \(m+1>\lambda_s^+\) imply \(\tau_m\to0\), while (30), (33), and (34) give \(\omega_h,\xi_s,\beta_s\to0\).

For the converse contraction, take an optimal rational lower-program rule.  Interpret \(\varnothing_G\) as a degenerate interval at any point of \(\mathcal A\) that is not a grid target; this has length zero and covers no grid target.  The directed rounding rules and (33) imply that its actual retained gridwise coverage is at least \(1-\alpha-\tau_m-\xi_s\), and its actual retained expected length is at most \(D_{m,h,s}^-+\xi_s\).  Report \(\mathcal A\) on overflow, expand retained intervals by \(bh/2\) at each endpoint, and use (26) from the nearest grid point.  The resulting rule has continuum coverage at least
\[
 1-\alpha-(\xi_s+\omega_h)                        \tag{37}
\]
and worst expected length at most
\[
 D_{m,h,s}^-+\xi_s+2br\tau_m+bh+2br\omega_h.      \tag{38}
\]
One repair (17) with \(u=\xi_s+\omega_h\) makes (37) honest.  Therefore
\[
 C_\alpha(\lambda)
 \le D_{m,h,s}^-+\xi_s+2br\tau_m+bh+2br\omega_h
 +\frac{2br(\xi_s+\omega_h)}{\alpha+\xi_s+\omega_h}. \tag{39}
\]
Equations (28), (30), and (33) show that every term following \(D_{m,h,s}^-\) in (39) vanishes along every declared refinement.  Combining (29), (36), and (39) proves
\[
 D_{m,h,s}^-\to C_\alpha(\lambda),\qquad
 U_{m,h,s}^+\to C_\alpha(\lambda),\qquad
 U_{m,h,s}^+-D_{m,h,s}^-\to0.                    \tag{40}
\]
In particular, at \(\lambda=1\) and \(\alpha=0.05\), every certified upper rule in a sufficiently fine refinement has coverage at least \(0.95\) on every segment, by (30)--(31), and the intersection hulls of successive valid brackets form a nonincreasing sequence of certified brackets with width tending to zero by (40).

Finally, the deterministic-array implementation is precisely the construction behind (20): transport the marked-Poisson upper rule through the deterministic collision statistic, pay at most \(d_K\) in coverage and \(2brd_K\) in expected length, and mix once with \(\mathcal A\) with probability \(d_K/(\alpha+d_K)\).  The lower comparison is precisely (19), using the parameter-free supported-mixture reverse kernel.  Thus both the exact interval-action certification and the two-sided honest-minimax transfer concern the realized sharp endpoint \(L_K\), uniformly over the full deterministic-array class.

added_lemmas.statement: In the independent and identically distributed Bernoulli-treatment design with overlap, compact covariate and outcome domains, and continuous cost \(h\), the sharp lower endpoint over causal couplings preserving the two conditional outcome laws is the conditional optimal-transport functional \(L(P)\) in (41).

attestation.note: The theorem locator and its compact-domain, continuous-cost scope are supplied by the frozen bibliography record and the active orchestrator directive; a stable public source handle is supplied in lieu of an unverified verbatim transcription.

added_lemmas.justification: Embedding the collision submodel into the paper's causal anchor makes the maximal valid transfer explicit: minimax converse bounds pass to every containing class by restriction.
added_lemmas.gap: The collision constructions establish upper bounds only on the deterministic-array experiment; subclass monotonicity gives lower bounds, but not upper bounds or equalities, on broader anchor-admissible classes.
added_lemmas.consumer: The result lets \(\texttt{causalPIviaCOT}\) treat the collision frontier as a certified obstruction for any analysis class containing the finite-grid stress test while retaining the narrower interpolation-only achievability scope.

proposed.statement: For every \((\theta_{dj})\in\mathcal T_K(r)\), the sharp lower bound on \(\mathbb E|Y(1)-Y(0)|\) over couplings preserving the two conditional Bernoulli laws cell by cell is \(L_K\), and \(L_K=a-b\rho_K\).
proposed.justification: This setup proposition fixes the actual causal partial-identification endpoint before any statistical approximation and provides a sanity check for the collision parameterization.
proposed.gap: This identity is a direct binary specialization of Lin, Gao, Blanchet, and Glynn's general sharp COT bound in Theorem~1; no novelty is claimed for the affine calculation.
proposed.consumer: The identity lets \(\texttt{causalPIviaCOT}\) interpret partition-resolution diagnostics directly as uncertainty about a sharp endpoint rather than about an auxiliary regression coefficient.

proposed_core_edits.reason: The proof interprets the uniform cell average as a functional of the full observable law, so its finite-array experiment dependency must be explicit.

proposed.comparator_claim: Theorem 1 gives general sharp conditional optimal-transport bounds on compact covariate and outcome domains with continuous objective, and Theorems 2--6 develop continuity and statistical guarantees for their estimation.

Proposition 3.2 supplies the key estimation bound, Proposition 3.3 supplies the quadratic-objective stability inequality, and Theorem 3.2 establishes asymptotic normality for quadratic COT under smooth positive densities.
Theorem 3.1 gives uniformly valid dual lower confidence bounds even under an arbitrarily inaccurate outcome model, while later results give sharpness under nuisance-rate conditions.

The public manuscript characterizes sharp optimal-transport identified intervals and gives root-n sample-analogue inference for potential-outcome functionals in an instrumental-variables noncompliance model.
Theorems 2.1 and 2.3 transfer a sharp multinomial-uniformity testing lower bound using supported Poisson mixtures and a conditional central limit theorem.
Theorem 1 and Corollary 1 characterize minimax expected-measure confidence sets through Bayes--minimax duality and test inversion.
Propositions 1 and 2 give uniformly valid confidence intervals for interval-identified parameters with explicit treatment of the identified-set-length nuisance.
Theorem 3 proves local asymptotic minimax efficiency of Bayes estimators in nonregular parameter-dependent-support experiments.
Theorem 1 bounds total-variation error for Poisson approximation of locally dependent rare-event counts and processes.
The published minimax analysis identifies collision-dominated behavior for testing uniformity of sparse Poisson data under missing-ball alternatives.
The coincidence statistic attains the sparse-alphabet sample-complexity threshold for uniformity testing through explicit collision moment bounds.
Poissonized and density-estimation experiments are asymptotically equivalent above a Besov regularity frontier and can fail to be equivalent below it.
Finite-sample optimal confidence intervals balance worst-case smoothness bias against variance for average treatment effects under unconfoundedness.

proposed_core_edits.reason: The comparator description must record the exact compact-domain and continuous-cost anchor used by the new converse while retaining the honest informed-by positioning rather than claiming an extension of the published theorem.

prose_updates.tldr: For binary outcomes on a growing uniform covariate partition, the sharp absolute-cost COT lower endpoint is \(L_K=a-b\rho_K\), with \(\rho_K\) the realized correlation of two deterministic sign arrays. When \(\lambda_K=n_0n_1/K\) stays finite and triple collisions vanish, a Poisson number of cross-arm collisions carries the minimax information: parameter-free supported-mixture kernels and a uniform deterministic-array collision approximation yield exact minimax absolute-risk and honest-length transfer, together with shrinking rational interval-action certificates whose tail, off-grid coverage, and rounding errors are explicit. When \(\lambda_K\) diverges sparsely, the unprojected estimator is uniformly studentized Gaussian and the matching deterministic-shell local minimax theorem gives the interior variance frontier. Embedding cell \(j\) as \(j/K\) shows that these finite and local frontiers are converse lower bounds for every anchor-admissible class containing the submodel; this transfer is converse-only. Achievability outside the arrays remains limited to the declared continuous growing-roughness interpolation image, because coarsening can change the endpoint without a separate bias bound.

project_justification.gap: Published COT theory supplies the general sharp conditional-transport endpoint and statistical guarantees under its own regularity regimes, but it does not characterize the marked-Poisson information experiment created by sparse cross-arm replication on a growing partition. Large-alphabet collision theory and confidence-set duality supply ingredients, not the two-arm realized endpoint, certified interval-action enclosure, deterministic-array transfer, or the maximal converse for every anchor class containing that submodel.
project_justification.niche: The missing object is a single information frontier indexed by expected cross-arm collisions: exact finite-information decisions when \(\lambda_K\) is bounded, Gaussian local efficiency when it diverges sparsely, and an explicit statement of which conclusions pass from the finite stress test to broader COT classes.
project_justification.fill: The project proves a marked-Poisson reduction with parameter-free forward and reverse randomization under shell-conditioned legal mixtures, derives uniform collision approximation for every deterministic array, certifies finite-information intervals by exact rational lower-dual and upper-primal witnesses with continuum coverage repair, and establishes the ordered LAN-to-deterministic-shell local minimax theorem. The finite arrays embed into the compact-domain Bernoulli-design COT anchor, so subclass monotonicity transfers both finite-intensity frontiers and the local truncated-quadratic variance as converse lower bounds to every containing class. Collision-based upper bounds are not claimed for those broader classes; continuous achievability remains confined to the explicit interpolation image.

prose_updates.related_work: Lin, Gao, Blanchet, and Glynn (2026, AISTATS, Theorems 1--6) establish general sharp COT bounds, continuity, and statistical guarantees. Their Theorem~1, under compact covariate and outcome domains and a continuous objective, is the identification anchor: the affine binary endpoint here is a directly proved specialization, and the embedded arrays satisfy that anchor setup. The new anchor-containing-class result transfers collision lower bounds upward only by submodel monotonicity; it does not claim that the collision procedures furnish upper bounds over Lin et al.'s broader class, and alternating embedded signs need not satisfy later uniform smoothness or rate hypotheses. Their smooth-density follow-up (2026) uses Proposition~3.2 for the key estimation bound, Proposition~3.3 for quadratic-objective stability, and Theorem~3.2 for asymptotic normality; atomic binary outcomes and absolute cost require different marked-collision likelihood theory. Ji, Lei, and Spector (2023, Theorems 3.1--3.5) provide model-agnostic dual inference and emphasize binning loss, but do not optimize honest expected length or identify the collision frontier. Ober-Reynolds (2023, arXiv:2311.09435) derives sharp OT intervals and root-\(n\) sample-analogue inference in an instrumental-variables noncompliance model, not sparse covariate collisions. Paninski (2008) and Kipnis (2026) show that collisions govern sparse large-alphabet testing; Kipnis's supported-mixture architecture is especially close, but its object is one-sample uniformity testing. Arratia, Goldstein, and Gordon (1989, Theorem~1) supply the dependency-neighborhood Poisson approximation. Evans, Hansen, and Stark (2005, Theorem~1 and Corollary~1) supply test inversion and Bayes--minimax duality, while Stoye (2009, Propositions~1--2) diagnoses boundary failures; neither supplies the tail truncation, likelihood modulus, endpoint expansion, full-interval repair, or exact rational verification used here. Hirano and Porter (2003, Theorem~3) provide a limit-experiment efficiency template; the completed supported-shell argument establishes the ordered deterministic-array local minimax theorem for bounded truncated quadratic losses. Low and Zhou (2007) and Armstrong and Kolesár (2021) motivate the restricted pushforward and bias-aware scope, without supporting an upper claim over a full smoothness ball.
prose_updates.honest_scope: The proved finite-\(\lambda\) comparison and decision theorems concern the realized endpoint \(L_K\) over the full legal deterministic-array class. The rational interval certificates cover computable \(\lambda\) and require outward-rounded likelihood, tail, action-length, primal, and dual checks; floating-point solver output alone remains outside the claim. The sparse theorem gives unprojected studentized Gaussian inference and the matching ordered deterministic-shell local minimax variance at interior correlations. The embedded finite-array laws meet the compact-domain, continuous-cost COT identification anchor, so their global and local minimax lower bounds transfer to every containing anchor-admissible class; this is a converse-only statement and supplies no collision-based upper bound or equality on a broader class. Continuous achievability transfers only through the declared interpolation-image pushforward. No raw total-variation comparison is made between mutually singular continuous covariates and discrete labels, and no claim is made for unknown amplitudes, nonuniform cell probabilities, nonnegligible triple collisions, dense cellwise estimation, or a full continuous smoothness class. Coarsening changes the estimand unless a separate bias theorem is supplied.

proofs.proof_tex:
For a legal deterministic array \(\theta=(\theta_{dj})\), let \(P^{\mathcal F}_{K,\theta}\) be the observable law of \(\mathcal O_K=((Z_{di},Y_{di}))_{d,i}\) specified by the uniform-label, independent-arm, and conditional-Bernoulli assumptions.  The array \(\theta\) is unobserved.  By Proposition \texttt{prop:sharp-cot-endpoint}, the causal target attached to this law is the sharp coupling endpoint
\[
 t_K(\theta):=L_K(\theta)=a-b\rho_K(\theta),
 \qquad
 \rho_K(\theta)=K^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^K\theta_{0j}\theta_{1j}.
 \tag{1}
\]
The marked-Poisson target is the distinct decision functional \(t(\rho):=a-b\rho\).  The supported mixtures below are used only to compare experiments; equation (1) and an explicit target-discrepancy bound relate their proxy target \(t(q)\) to the realized causal target.

The proof uses bounded-loss total-variation comparison, a supported-mixture reduction for the lower bound, and explicit couplings for changes in the marked-Poisson parameter and intensity.  First note the following elementary bounded-loss fact.  If probability measures \(P,Q\) are on the same measurable space and \(0\le g\le B\), then the layer-cake representation gives
\[
 \left|\int g\,dP-\int g\,dQ\right|
 \le \int_0^B\left|P\{g>u\}-Q\{g>u\}\right|\,du
 \le B\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}.
 \tag{2}
\]
The same argument applied to the functions supplied by a Markov kernel proves contraction of total variation under randomization.  Because every target in this proof belongs to \(\mathcal A=[a-br,a+br]\), projection of an endpoint action onto \(\mathcal A\) cannot increase absolute loss.  Thus all rules may be taken to have values in \(\mathcal A\), and then their absolute loss is bounded by \(2br\).

Define the deterministic-statistic and supported-mixture errors
\[
 d_K:=\min\left\{1,5\varepsilon_K+\frac{\lambda_K^2}{2K}\right\},
 \qquad
 e_K:=\min\{1,5\varepsilon_K+\eta_K\},
 \tag{3}
\]
and put
\[
 \delta_K:=2s_K+\frac2K,
 \qquad
 \omega_K:=\min\left\{1,\frac{\lambda_Kc\delta_K}{2}\right\}.
 \tag{4}
\]

We first obtain an upper comparison over all legal deterministic arrays.  Let \(D_\lambda\in\mathscr D_{\lambda_K}\) be any marked-Poisson rule, projected onto \(\mathcal A\), and apply it to the positive- and negative-mark counts extracted from \((M_K,S_1,\ldots,S_{M_K})\).  This is a single measurable finite-array rule and does not depend on \(\theta\).  For every \(\theta\in\mathcal T_K(r)\), the deterministic part of Theorem \texttt{thm:collision-comparison}, (1), (2), and (3) yield
\[
 \mathbb E_\theta\left|D_\lambda-L_K(\theta)\right|
 \le
 \mathbb E_{\lambda_K,\rho_K(\theta)}
 \left|D_\lambda-t(\rho_K(\theta))\right|+2brd_K.
 \tag{5}
\]
Taking the supremum over \(\theta\), then the infimum over \(D_\lambda\), gives the finite-sample upper comparison
\[
 R_K\le R(\lambda_K)+2brd_K.
 \tag{6}
\]
Thus the upper bound uses only the deterministic collision statistic and targets the realized endpoint in (1).

For the reverse comparison, fix an arbitrary finite-array rule \(D_K\in\mathscr D_K\), again projected onto \(\mathcal A\), and denote its maximal deterministic-array risk by
\[
 \mathcal R_K(D_K):=sup_{\theta\in\mathcal T_K(r)}
 \mathbb E_\theta|D_K-L_K(\theta)|.
 \tag{7}
\]
For all sufficiently large \(K\), Proposition \texttt{prop:supported-mixture-legality} makes \(\mathcal R_K^{\circ}(r)\) nonempty.  For each \(q\) in that lattice, the mixture is supported on \(\mathcal T_K(r)\) and satisfies \(|L_K(\theta)-t(q)|\le bs_K\) throughout its support.  The definition of expectation under the mixture law and the triangle inequality therefore give
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \mathbb E_{P^{\mathrm{mix}}_{K,q}}|D_K-t(q)|
 &=\int \mathbb E_\theta|D_K-t(q)|\,
      d\Pi^{\mathrm{shell}}_{K,q}(\theta)\\
 &\le \int\!\left\{
       \mathbb E_\theta|D_K-L_K(\theta)|
       +|L_K(\theta)-t(q)|\right\}
       d\Pi^{\mathrm{shell}}_{K,q}(\theta)\\
 &\le \mathcal R_K(D_K)+bs_K.
\end{aligned}
\tag{8}
\]
Compose \(D_K\) with the parameter-free reverse kernel \(\mathsf K_K^{\leftarrow}\) supplied by Theorem \texttt{thm:collision-comparison}, and call the resulting single marked-Poisson rule \(\widetilde D_K\).  The supported-mixture part of that theorem, (2), (3), and (8) imply, uniformly over \(q\in\mathcal R_K^{\circ}(r)\),
\[
 \mathbb E_{\lambda_K,q}|\widetilde D_K-t(q)|
 \le \mathcal R_K(D_K)+bs_K+2bre_K.
 \tag{9}
\]

It remains to pass from the interior lattice to all \(\rho\in[-r,r]\).  Set \(q=q_K(\rho)\), so that Proposition \texttt{prop:supported-mixture-legality} gives \(|q-\rho|\le\delta_K\).  Couple \(\mathcal E_{\lambda_K,\rho}\) and \(\mathcal E_{\lambda_K,q}\) by using the same \(N\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda_K)\) and the same independent uniform variables for their marks.  A single mark differs with probability
\[
 \left|\frac{1+c\rho}{2}-\frac{1+cq}{2}\right|
 =\frac c2|\rho-q|.
\]
Conditional on \(N\), a union bound, followed by expectation, therefore shows that the entire marked observations disagree with probability at most
\[
 \min\left\{1,\mathbb E[N]\frac c2|\rho-q|\right\}
 \le \omega_K.
 \tag{10}
\]
Consequently their total-variation distance is at most \(\omega_K\).  Since \(|t(\rho)-t(q)|=b|\rho-q|\le b\delta_K\), equations (2), (9), and (10) give
\[
 \mathbb E_{\lambda_K,\rho}|\widetilde D_K-t(\rho)|
 \le \mathcal R_K(D_K)+b(s_K+\delta_K)
       +2br(e_K+\omega_K).
 \tag{11}
\]
Taking the supremum over \(\rho\in[-r,r]\), using \(\widetilde D_K\) as an admissible rule in the definition of \(R(\lambda_K)\), and then taking the infimum over \(D_K\), proves
\[
 R(\lambda_K)
 \le R_K+b(s_K+\delta_K)+2br(e_K+\omega_K).
 \tag{12}
\]
This establishes the lower comparison using only mixtures supported on legal deterministic arrays.  In particular, no mixture target has been substituted for \(L_K\): the two discrepancies are paid explicitly in (8) and (11).

We next prove continuity of the limit decision frontier.  For \(\lambda,\lambda'\ge0\) and fixed \(\rho\), couple the two marked Poisson processes by retaining a common process of intensity \(\min\{\lambda,\lambda'\}\) and adding an independent process of intensity \(|\lambda-\lambda'|\) to the larger one, with all points marked according to \((1+c\rho)/2\).  The observations agree whenever the added process is empty, so, uniformly in \(\rho\),
\[
 \left\|P^{\mathcal E}_{\lambda,\rho}
       -P^{\mathcal E}_{\lambda',\rho}\right\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
 \le 1-e^{-|\lambda-\lambda'|}
 \le |\lambda-\lambda'|.
 \tag{13}
\]
Both experiments have the same count space and the same target \(t(\rho)\).  Applying (2) to any projected rule, then taking the parameter supremum and the rule infimum in both directions, yields
\[
 |R(\lambda)-R(\lambda')|
 \le 2br\bigl(1-e^{-|\lambda-\lambda'|}\bigr).
 \tag{14}
\]
Hence \(R\) is continuous on \([0,\infty)\), including at zero.

Finally suppose \(\lambda_K\to\lambda<\infty\).  By Lemma \texttt{lem:vanishing-triples-implies-growing-cells}, \(K\to\infty\).  Since \((\lambda_K)\) is bounded, the definition of \(s_K\) gives, for all sufficiently large \(K\),
\[
 s_K=\{K(1\vee\lambda_K)\}^{-1/4}\longrightarrow0,
 \qquad
 Ks_K^2=\sqrt{\frac{K}{1\vee\lambda_K}}\longrightarrow\infty.
 \tag{15}
\]
Thus \(\eta_K=2e^{-Ks_K^2/2}\to0\).  The vanishing-triples assumption, boundedness of \(\lambda_K\), and (3)--(4) now imply
\[
 e_K\to0,
 \qquad d_K\to0,
 \qquad \delta_K\to0,
 \qquad \omega_K\to0.
 \tag{16}
\]
By (14), \(R(\lambda_K)\to R(\lambda)\).  The upper and lower comparisons (6) and (12), together with (16), squeeze \(R_K\) to \(R(\lambda)\).  Therefore
\[
 R_K\longrightarrow R(\lambda).
\]

proposed.statement: If \(\lambda_K\to\lambda\in[0,\infty)\), then \(R_K\to R(\lambda)\). The lower bound ranges over supported mixtures on legal deterministic arrays, and the upper bound uses only the deterministic collision statistic; both sides target the realized \(L_K\).
proposed.justification: The theorem converts a nonregular finite-array estimation problem into an exact one-parameter decision frontier.
proposed.gap: Kipnis obtains sharp minimax risk for large-alphabet testing, not absolute-error estimation of an affine COT endpoint over deterministic two-arm arrays.
proposed.consumer: A partition designer can report the irreducible estimation error implied by the expected number of cross-arm replications.

proposed_core_edits.reason: The proof directly invokes the sharp endpoint identity, so its proposition must be a direct declared dependency.

proofs.proof_tex:
We give the local lower and upper arguments separately and keep the order of limits explicit.

First derive the local limit experiment.  Fix \(\rho _0\in(-r,r)\), and put
\[
 u_+=1+c\rho _0,\qquad u_-=1-c\rho _0,
 \qquad I_0=\frac{c^2}{1-c^2\rho _0^2}.
\]
The amplitude and correlation restrictions give \(0<c<1\) and \(|\rho _0|<r<1\), so \(u_+\) and \(u_-\) are strictly positive.  By the definition of the marked-Poisson experiment, under \(\mathcal E_{\lambda_K,\rho _0}\) the counts \(N_+\) and \(N_-\) are independent Poisson variables with respective means \(\lambda_Ku_+/2\) and \(\lambda_Ku_-/2\).  For \(\rho=\rho _0+h/\sqrt{\lambda_K}\), Taylor expansion of the displayed exact mass \(f_{\lambda_K,\rho}\) gives, uniformly for \(h\) in a fixed compact set,
\[
 \log\frac{f_{\lambda_K,\rho}}{f_{\lambda_K,\rho _0}}
 =h\Delta_K-\frac12h^2I_0+o_{P_{\rho _0}}(1),
 \qquad
 \Delta_K=\frac c{\sqrt{\lambda_K}}
 \left(\frac{N_+}{u_+}-\frac{N_-}{u_-}\right).
 \tag{20}
\]
Indeed,
\[
 \mathbb E_{\rho _0}\Delta_K=0,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{Var}_{\rho _0}(\Delta_K)
 =\frac{c^2}{2}\left(\frac1{u_+}+\frac1{u_-}\right)
 =I_0,
\]
the centered Poisson characteristic functions give
\(\Delta_K\rightsquigarrow\mathcal N(0,I_0)\), and the third-order Taylor remainder is \(O_{P_{\rho _0}}(\lambda_K^{-1/2})\) on every compact \(h\)-set because \(u_+\wedge u_->0\).  If \(\Lambda_{K,h}\) denotes the likelihood ratio in (20), direct use of the Poisson exponential-moment formula yields
\[
 \mathbb E_{\rho _0}\Lambda_{K,h}^{,2}
 =\exp\left\{\frac{c^2h^2}{2}
 \left(\frac1{u_+}+\frac1{u_-}\right)\right\}
 =e^{h^2I_0}.
\]
Thus the likelihood ratios are uniformly integrable on every compact \(h\)-set.  For every finite collection of local parameters, (20), the preceding second-moment bound, and the continuous mapping theorem therefore imply convergence of every bounded finite-prior Bayes risk to that in the Gaussian location experiment
\[
 X=-bh+\sqrt{V(\rho _0)}Z,
 \qquad Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1),
 \tag{21}
\]
whose target is \(-bh\).  The variance identity follows from the declared relation \(c=4ab\):
\[
 \frac{b^2}{I_0}
 =\frac{b^2(1-c^2\rho _0^2)}{c^2}
 =\frac{1-c^2\rho _0^2}{16a^2}
 =V(\rho _0).
 \tag{22}
\]
More explicitly, after domination by the central law, the Bayes risk under a finite prior is the expectation of the pointwise infimum, over the action, of a finite weighted sum of bounded losses multiplied by likelihood ratios.  That infimum is Lipschitz in the likelihood-ratio vector with constant at most \(T\); convergence in distribution together with the displayed uniform-integrability bound gives convergence of its expectation.  This proves the finite-prior risk assertion without transferring an unbounded loss.  Also, since \(\rho _0\in(-r,r)\) and \(\mathcal A\subset\mathcal D\), the scaled action image \(\sqrt{\lambda_K}\{\mathcal D-(a-b\rho _0)\}\) exhausts \(\mathbb R\).  Restricting finite-sample actions to that image can only increase the lower Bayes bound.

We next calculate the minimax value of (21) under the bounded loss.  Let \(Z_V\sim\mathcal N(0,V(\rho _0))\), let \(\varphi_V\) be its density, and define
\[
 m_T=\mathbb E\min\{Z_V^2,T\}.
\]
The translation-equivariant rule \(X\) has constant risk \(m_T\).  Conversely, average the risk of any rule in the Gaussian location experiment against the uniform prior on the target interval \([-A,A]\).  For \(0<B<A\), restricting the observation integral to \([-A+B,A-B]\) and changing variables gives the lower bound
\[
 \left(1-\frac BA\right)
 \inf_{v\in\mathbb R}
 \int_{-B}^{B}\ell_T(v+z)\varphi_V(z)\,dz.
 \tag{23}
\]
For completeness, the layer-cake identity
\[
 \ell_T(x)=\int_0^T {\bf 1}\{|x|>\sqrt t\}\,dt
\]
shows that the last integral is minimized at \(v=0\): for every \(t\), a centered interval of the prescribed length has the largest mass under the symmetric unimodal density \(\varphi_V(z){\bf 1}\{|z|\le B\}\).  Letting first \(A\to\infty\) and then \(B\to\infty\), monotone convergence makes (23) tend to \(m_T\).  Hence the Gaussian minimax value is \(m_T\).  Moreover, Gaussian shifts are continuous in total variation in their location, and \(\ell_T\) is bounded and continuous.  Approximating the preceding compact uniform priors by finite grids shows that, for every \(\delta>0\), there is a finite prior supported on target values in some \([-bG,bG]\) whose Gaussian Bayes risk is at least \(m_T-\delta\).  Equivalently, its local \(h\)-support is contained in \([-G,G]\).

We now transfer such a finite prior to supported mixtures over legal deterministic arrays.  Since \(n_0,n_1\) are positive integers, the definition of \(\varepsilon_K\) implies, for \(d=0,1\),
\[
 \varepsilon_K
 =\frac{n_0n_1(n_0+n_1)}{K^2}
 \ge \left(\frac{n_d}{K}\right)^2.
\]
The vanishing-triples assumption therefore gives \(n_d/K\to0\), and hence
\[
 \frac{\lambda_K}{K}
 =\frac{n_0}{K}\frac{n_1}{K}\longrightarrow0.
\]
Together with \(\lambda_K\to\infty\), the definition of \(s_K\) then gives eventually
\[
 s_K=(K\lambda_K)^{-1/4},
 \qquad
 \sqrt{\lambda_K}s_K
 =\left(\frac{\lambda_K}{K}\right)^{1/4}\longrightarrow0,
 \qquad
 Ks_K^2=\sqrt{\frac K{\lambda_K}}\longrightarrow\infty.
 \tag{24}
\]
Consequently \(\eta_K=2e^{-Ks_K^2/2}\to0\), and the collision-comparison error \(e_K=\min\{1,5\varepsilon_K+\eta_K\}\) tends to zero.  The projection inequality in the supported-mixture legality proposition also gives, uniformly over \(|h|\le G\),
\[
 \sqrt{\lambda_K}\left|
 q_K\left(\rho _0+\frac h{\sqrt{\lambda_K}}\right)
 -\rho _0-\frac h{\sqrt{\lambda_K}}
 \right|
 \le 2\sqrt{\lambda_K}s_K+\frac{2\sqrt{\lambda_K}}K
 \longrightarrow0.
 \tag{25}
\]
Here the arguments of \(q_K\) lie in \([-r,r]\) for all sufficiently large \(K\), because \(\rho _0\) is interior and \(G\) is fixed.

For each support point \(h\) of the finite prior, use the mixing law
\[
 \Pi_{K,q_K(\rho _0+h/\sqrt{\lambda_K})}^{\mathrm{shell}}.
\]
By its defining shell event, (24), and (25), for every fixed \(H>G+1\), the support of every one of these mixtures is contained in \(\mathcal H_K(\rho _0,H)\) for all sufficiently large \(K\).  The supported-mixture legality proposition and the sharp endpoint identity give the uniform realized-target comparison
\[
 \sqrt{\lambda_K}
 \left|L_K-\left(a-bq_K\left(\rho _0+\frac h{\sqrt{\lambda_K}}\right)\right)\right|
 \le b\sqrt{\lambda_K}s_K\longrightarrow0.
 \tag{26}
\]
The map \(x\mapsto\ell_T(x)\) is \(2\sqrt T\)-Lipschitz, so replacing the realized target in each mixture by its attached target changes risk by \(o(1)\), uniformly on this finite prior.

Let \(D_K\in\mathscr D_K\) be arbitrary.  Compose it with the parameter-free reverse kernel supplied by the collision-comparison theorem.  The resulting marked-Poisson rule has finite-prior Bayes risk no greater than the full-data mixture Bayes risk plus \(Te_K+o(1)\).  The latter mixture Bayes risk is at most the supremum of the deterministic-array risks over \(\mathcal H_K(\rho _0,H)\), because all mixing laws are supported there.  Equations (20), (25), and (26), finite-prior Bayes-risk convergence, and the choice of the finite prior therefore yield
\[
 \liminf_{K\to\infty}
 \inf_{D_K\in\mathscr D_K}
 \sup_{\theta\in\mathcal H_K(\rho _0,H)}
 \mathbb E_\theta\ell_T\!\left(
 \sqrt{\lambda_K}(D_K-L_K)\right)
 \ge m_T-\delta
\]
for every fixed \(T\) and every sufficiently large fixed \(H>G+1\).  Letting \(H\to\infty\) and then \(\delta\downarrow0\) proves the ordered-limit lower bound \(m_T\).

For the upper bound, the uniform sparse-Gaussian theorem and the shell relation
\(\sup_{\theta\in\mathcal H_K(\rho _0,H)}|\rho_K-\rho _0|\le H/\sqrt{\lambda_K}\) imply, for every fixed \(H,T\),
\[
 \limsup_{K\to\infty}
 \sup_{\theta\in\mathcal H_K(\rho _0,H)}
 \mathbb E_\theta\ell_T\!\left(
 \sqrt{\lambda_K}(\widehat L_K-L_K)\right)
 \le \mathbb E\ell_T\!\left(\sqrt{V(\rho _0)}Z\right)
 =m_T.
 \tag{27}
\]
Indeed, studentization and uniform consistency of \(\widehat V_K\) give uniform weak convergence of the unstudentized quantity to \(\mathcal N(0,V(\rho _0))\), and bounded continuity of \(\ell_T\) then gives (27).  The distance from \(a-b\rho _0\) to the boundary of \(\mathcal D=[a-b,a+b]\) is strictly positive.  On a fixed shell, (27) implies uniform \(\lambda_K^{-1/2}\)-consistency, so the probability that clipping is active tends uniformly to zero.  Because the loss is bounded by \(T\), (27) therefore also holds with \(\operatorname{clip}_{\mathcal D}(\widehat L_K)\) in place of \(\widehat L_K\).

The lower bound and (27) show that the inner ordered limit equals \(m_T\).  Finally, only after taking \(K\to\infty\) and then \(H\to\infty\), monotone convergence in \(T\) gives
\[
 \lim_{T\to\infty}m_T
 =\mathbb E Z_V^2
 =V(\rho _0).
\]
This proves the displayed ordered identity and both estimator assertions.  At no stage is an unbounded scaled loss transferred through total variation; the Poisson approximation enters only through the frozen collision-comparison theorem and its declared aggregate Poisson-approximation dependency.
